solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Alternative grassed areas — that's usual

definitions.meaning: a choice between two kinds of lawn: the village green held in common, or the plot behind a house

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that choosing between two patches of lawn is the normal state of affairs.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the phrase literally: one grassy space OR another, the shared green or the private one.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes anything ordinary and unremarkable, so it matches a word for typical.

clue.text: French epic showing 100 desecrated headstones including separate parts for English

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

indicators.note: desecrated says the headstones are knocked about, so their letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: Vandals spoil a hundred gravestones, picking out English ones.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'including separate parts for English' has no single device: it means the abbreviation's letters are scattered through the jumble rather than kept together.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a medieval French epic poem about heroic deeds, such as the Song of Roland.

clue.text: Actress serving men with real full-flavoured planned food, first

indicators.note: first places the food piece before the flavour piece
serving suggests the letters are dished up in a new arrangement

parts.note: a diet is a planned eating regime
rich food is full-flavoured

explanation.surface: A star served a meal of men and rich food, with a diet coming first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'serving' looks like the meal on the surface but signals the anagram; 'first' reverses the clue's order for the last two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: She was a German-born Hollywood film star of the 1930s, famous for The Blue Angel.

clue.text: Finger — when the top's missing, that hurts!

indicators.note: the top's missing says the first letter is removed, the top in a down entry

parts.note: to finger something is to touch it

explanation.surface: Someone with a damaged finger whose tip has gone cries out in pain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finger' looks like a noun but is the verb, meaning to touch.
explanation.definitionFit: The interjection is the standard cry of sudden pain.

clue.text: Cost of exchanging model railway components

indicators.note: exchanging swaps the two halves of the railway word, the back part coming to the front

parts.note: a layout is the arrangement of track and scenery, the components of a model railway

explanation.surface: The price of swapping parts on a model railway.
explanation.walkthrough: LAYOUT, the word for a model railway set-up, has its two parts LAY and OUT swapped.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun means money spent, an expenditure or cost.

clue.text: Familiar fruit that's good with eggs — mixed with three eggs

indicators.note: mixed with says the letters are stirred together into a new order

parts.note: an egg is O for its shape, so three eggs give three Os

explanation.surface: A recipe mixing fruit with a good number of eggs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Familiar' marks a colloquial word: this is British slang for gooseberry.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an informal British name for the gooseberry, so the fruit by its familiar name.

clue.text: Bird out west around edge on these French homes

indicators.note: around says the trimmed bird encloses the edge
out says the west letter leaves the bird

parts.note: the wren is a small songbird
W is the compass abbreviation for west
a side is an edge
ces is French for these

explanation.surface: A bird flies away westwards around the edge of these French houses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out west' reads like a direction of flight, but 'out' removes the west letter, leaving REN; 'on' is just a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean places where people live, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Critic (see column) savaged Stockhausen's work?

indicators.note: savaged says the words are torn apart, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A newspaper critic tore apart a piece by the composer Stockhausen in his column.
explanation.walkthrough: 'savaged' shuffles CRITIC, SEE and COLUMN; the question mark flags the definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Karlheinz Stockhausen was a pioneer of electronically generated sound, so his output exemplifies the genre.

clue.text: Novel start to historical work

definitions.meaning: Evelyn Waugh's first novel, published in 1928
the opening words of Edward Gibbon's history of the Roman Empire's collapse

explanation.surface: A new way to begin a history book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like the adjective for new, but it is the noun: Waugh's book. Gibbon's work is The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is both a Waugh title and the first words of Gibbon's great history.

clue.text: A soft cheese? No thanks. Fruit please

parts.note: P is piano, the musical marking for playing softly

indicators.note: No in front of thanks says to go without those letters, dropping them from the cheese

parts.note: ricotta is a soft Italian cheese
TA is British informal for thank you

explanation.surface: A diner turns down a cheese course and asks for some fruit instead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No thanks' takes TA off RICOTTA, leaving RICOT; 'please' is only surface politeness.
explanation.definitionFit: An apricot is a small orange stone fruit, an example of the category named.

clue.text: Hideous outside broadcast by Panorama

parts.note: OB is the standard abbreviation for a broadcast from outside the studio
a panorama is a view or scene

explanation.surface: Panorama, the BBC current-affairs programme, puts out something ugly from an outside broadcast.
explanation.walkthrough: Panorama looks like the BBC programme, tying in with the broadcast, but it just means a view.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something offensive and revolting, so they are loose synonyms.

clue.text: Asymmetrical gardens — first add topsoil?

indicators.note: first add means this piece is put before the rest

parts.note: the top letter of soil is S
Kew Gardens is the botanic garden in south-west London

explanation.surface: A gardener asks whether the first job is to spread topsoil on the beds.
explanation.walkthrough: KEW is the Royal Botanic Gardens in London. 'topsoil' means the top of 'soil', the letter S.
explanation.definitionFit: Something askew is slanted or lopsided, so the word is a synonym for unbalanced in shape.

clue.text: Lead actors dressed for the priesthood?

indicators.note: dressed suggests the letters are put into a new arrangement, like actors arranged in costume

explanation.surface: The leading cast members are costumed as clergy for a production.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dressed' signals the anagram of LEAD ACTORS.
explanation.definitionFit: This adjective means relating to priests, so it describes what is for the priesthood.

clue.text: Theatrical flower penniless hubby's got by cutter

indicators.note: penniless says the old penny, D, is removed

parts.note: old man is informal for husband
one who rives or splits things is a river

explanation.surface: A stage florist, a broke husband, gets help from someone with a blade.
explanation.walkthrough: D is the old British penny (from Latin denarius). A 'flower' in crosswords can be a river, something that flows.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous song from the stage musical Show Boat is about the Mississippi, a flowing river.

clue.text: Lionel adapted ornamental engraving

indicators.note: adapted says the name's letters are altered into a new order

explanation.surface: A man called Lionel modifies a decorative engraving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'adapted' signals the anagram of LIONEL.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a black metallic inlay used to fill engraved designs in silver, a decorative engraving technique.

clue.text: Shopping and business area in a certain Newcastle?

definitions.meaning: the commercial centre of a city, chiefly American usage
there is a Newcastle in County Down, Northern Ireland, so it is a town in Down

explanation.surface: A question about where the city centre is in Newcastle.
explanation.walkthrough: Newcastle suggests the city on the Tyne, but the one meant is the seaside town in County Down, Northern Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is the usual North American name for a city's central commercial district.

clue.text: Impressive quality of cleaner — one's mother

parts.note: a char is a cleaning lady in British usage
one is I, and the apostrophe s stands for is
ma is mother

explanation.surface: A household cleaner happens to be someone's mum.
explanation.walkthrough: A char (charwoman) is an old British term for a domestic cleaner.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means compelling personal magnetism, a quality that impresses others.

clue.text: Not happiest mementoes

indicators.note: Not in front of happiest says that word is not as written, so its letters must be rearranged

explanation.surface: Souvenirs that bring back memories of less than joyful times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not' is the anagram signal for HAPPIEST.
explanation.definitionFit: Words carved on a tombstone are reminders of the dead, so mementoes is a loose, wry definition.

clue.text: Tissue to remove bit of scum from wine

indicators.note: to remove says letters are taken out of the wine

parts.note: retsina is a Greek white wine flavoured with pine resin

indicators.note: bit of picks only the opening letter of scum

explanation.surface: Using a tissue to skim a bit of scum off the top of a glass of wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bit of scum' is S; 'to remove' takes it out of RETSINA.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the light-sensitive layer of tissue at the back of the eye.

clue.text: I am leaving judge's property

indicators.note: leaving says those letters go out of the judge word

parts.note: to estimate something is to judge it
I am contracts to I'M

explanation.surface: Someone declares they are walking away from a judge's land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'judge' looks like a person but is the verb, meaning to estimate.
explanation.definitionFit: An estate is a large area of land or all the possessions someone owns.

clue.text: Endeavour to put down with force

parts.note: to put down in a record is to enter it
to prise is to force open with a lever

explanation.surface: An attempt to suppress something by strength.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endeavour' and 'put down' look like verbs here, but the definition is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words name a bold undertaking or project, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Surrounded by a number in support

indicators.note: in places the number inside the support word

parts.note: aid means help or support
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand

explanation.surface: Someone backed up and hemmed in by a crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: M is the Roman numeral 1000, one of several numbers that crosswords use for single letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The preposition means in the middle of, the same as being encircled by things.

clue.text: Tangle with leader on Kawasaki doing 100mph?

indicators.note: leader on picks the first letter of the motorbike name
doing a ton is the slang phrase; here doing points to the speed word written up the column, backwards

parts.note: a ton is 100mph in motoring slang

explanation.surface: A tangle involving a speeding Kawasaki motorbike rider.
explanation.walkthrough: Bikers call 100mph 'a ton', and 'doing a ton' is the phrase; 'doing' sends the speed word backwards, giving NOT, up this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A knot is a twisted tangle in thread or hair, so it is a synonym.

clue.text: Thick fellows, endlessly calm during this

indicators.note: during places one piece inside the other
endlessly says the last letter is cut off

parts.note: even means calm, as in an even temper

explanation.surface: Some stupid men stay serene through all of this.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' leaves EVE, set 'during' the other word. 'Thick' means stupid on the surface but recalls the idiom 'thick as thieves'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'as thick as thieves' means very close, so the robbers are the proverbially thick fellows.

clue.text: Trouble with names one's beginning to admit

definitions.text: Trouble with names one's beginning to admit

indicators.note: Trouble with says the letters are disturbed and fall into a new order

parts.note: one is I in Roman numerals

indicators.note: beginning to picks the opening letter of admit

explanation.surface: Someone owning up that they are starting to forget people's names.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trouble with' shuffles NAMES and I into AMNESI, then 'beginning to admit' adds A.
explanation.definitionFit: Memory loss leaves you unable to recall what people are called, a condition one starts to confess.

clue.text: Concerned with medicines from Utah plc, America

indicators.note: from suggests the answer is made out of the following letters, reworked

explanation.surface: A drugs business registered as a plc in Utah, America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' is the anagram signal for UTAH PLC AMERICA.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes anything relating to drugs and their preparation.
